stochastic surrogate modelling of well placement

Keywords:
Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (ATES)
Well placement
Stochastic modelling
ATES in urban areas
Optimal use of subsurface
Heat recovery factor
 A B S T R A C T
Hot Temperature Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (HT-ATES) systems have gained interest due to their high 
storage capacity, cost-effectiveness, and environmental sustainability.  Especially in urban areas with surplus 
heat, geothermal district heating becomes highly beneficial.Wells in ATES must be spaced to avoid thermal 
interference, but urban space and regulations often constrain well placement. In this numerical study, we 
provide placement criteria for well doublets in urban areas.  In contrast to previous model approaches, 
the approach optimizes the trade-off between thermal interference and well spacing by maximizing energy 
recovery and minimizing well distance  To minimize computational costs, we designed a workflow where 
the full order physics-based model was replaced by a Random Forest Classifier (RFC) that predicts thermal 
interference with 97% accuracy accounting for technical and geological uncertainties in a typical deep HT-
ATES system.  The model was applied to an ATES system planned in Berlin-Adlershof. Results show that the 
well distance between 130 and 160 meters is optimal from the thermal and hydraulic perspective over a wide 
range of parameters. The global sensitivity analysis of the surrogate model reveals that influential parameters 
for thermal interference are well placement, aquifer thickness, flowrates, charging temperature, permeability, 
and porosity. By providing insights into key design priorities and enabling an explicit understanding of 
thermal interference, the developed RFC is an efficient tool for pre-evaluating possible ATES configurations 
and supporting urban planners’ decision making.
1. Introduction
Decarbonization and elimination of  greenhouse gas emissions have 
been in focus of the United Nations society since the last 20 years [1]. 
As one of the solutions, HT-ATES systems are an effective and rela-
tively low-cost technology for reusing and storing energy [2]. HT-ATES 
enables high-efficiency, seasonal thermal energy storage while offering 
low operational cost, minimal land use, and near-zero emissions, which 
makes it a scalable and cost-effective solution for integrating into 
district heating and cooling systems.
In high temperature ATES systems, excessive heated water is in-
jected into the subsurface in the summer time while the colder water is 
extracted for cooling the system. During winter, the process is reversed: 
the previously injected hot water is extracted from production wells 
and circulated through heat exchangers to heat buildings, with the 
cold water being reinjected into the aquifer. This ATES technology has 
been successfully implemented in over 1000 sites worldwide, mainly 
in the Netherlands [3], delivering an attractive alternative to carbon 
energy sources. Especially in urban areas which are characterized by

in the energy storage [see e.g.4,5].
While the appeal of energy storage with ATES is significant, its 
successful implementation requires a thorough understanding of sub-
surface properties, alongside a careful planning and management of 
technical solutions [1,6]. Several analytical solutions and key perfor-
mance characteristics have been developed to evaluate the efficiency 
of an ATES project [7,8], among those the most widely used is the 
Heat Recovery Factor (HRF) [9–11]. Physics-based numerical models 
are typically used for simulation of complex natural conditions such 
as aquifer heterogeneity and reactive behaviour [12–14], prediction of 
ATES efficiency under various ambient flow conditions [15] both at the 
district scale [16] and city scale [17], as well as targeting interacting 
systems [18]. The typical outcome of such models are temperature 
and pressure evolution curves over the whole lifetime of ATES system, 
which allows a proper quantification of the extracted energy and 
aquifer performance.

From a design perspective, natural parameters such as aquifer prop-
erties (porosity, permeability, aquifer thickness, thermal conductivity, 
and heat capacity) and relatively low ambient flow velocity are neces-
sary for high ATES efficiency [5,19–21]. At the same time, technical 
parameters such as distance between wells, charging temperature and 
flowrate, and duration of injection and extraction cycles define the 
boundary conditions to be operated in the injection and extraction 
wells [22–24].
To ensure optimal performance and efficiency, both natural and 
technical parameters of ATES systems have to be carefully estimated
[25]. Sommer et al. [26] highlighted the importance of an optimal 
well spacing. Recent modelling studies [27,28] demonstrated the rel-
evance of the optimization of the initial ATES design, which entails 
an accurate characterization of the system’s parameters. Besides tech-
nical design parameters, natural aquifer parameters, are influenced by 
various uncertainties due to limited subsurface data [29,30].
The ensemble-based stochastic modelling has shown its capability 
in uncertainty reduction and decision making [29,31]. The challenge 
of stochastic approaches is the high computational cost of a single 
simulation. To overcome the bottleneck of the high computational 
cost of stochastic simulations on a spatially resolved hydraulic–thermal 
model, surrogate modelling approaches have been developed [32,33]. 
Regression-based surrogate models were used to target different ques-
tions of optimal design [8,34–37] and sensitivity analysis [38]. Rohmer 
et al. [19] proposed using multifidelity cokriging approach for fast 
yet accurate ATES characterization for technical ATES parameters and 
aquifer properties to predict the evolution of well temperatures for dif-
ferent aquifer properties. By using a surrogate modelling approach [28] 
were able to determine optimal production rate for a site in crystalline 
rocks.
Despite significant advancements in uncertainty quantification and 
regression analysis for optimizing ATES design, only limited amount of 
studies focused on the optimal well spacing by accounting for both tech-
nical and natural uncertainties [8,39,40]. Current design approaches 
often rely on generalized analytical equations such as multiplied ther-
mal radius [26,27] and only define the minimum distance between the 
wells while ignoring the maximum distance estimation.
This study aims to bridge this gap by newly introducing both 
hydraulic and thermal criteria on the well placement in the HT-ATES 
doublet. While the thermal criteria define the minimum distance be-
tween the wells, the hydraulic criteria are capable to determine the 
maximum distance, thus leading to the range of possible distances 
for the doublet system. Based on an ensemble of spatially resolved 
numerical models, we confirmed the hypothesis of asymptotic devel-
opment of HRF over the broad parameter ranges, and suggested a 
possible analytical form of it. To speed up the model evaluation, we 
developed a model reduction technique that retains the complexity 
of full-scale models while facilitating efficient predictions. We used 
the key characteristic of the reduced physics-based model to create a 
computationally effective surrogate model. To predict ATES efficiency 
and optimize the well distance, a Random Forest Classifier [40,41] was 
trained on an ensemble of 1500 spatially resolved numerical models. 
The methodology was applied to an ATES project in Berlin, Germany, 
where spatial constraints and regulatory requirements make optimal 
well placement crucial for system success. The outcome was compared 
with the conventionally used thermal radius approach for the well 
distance selection. The results offer a scalable solution for ATES design 
in similar urban contexts globally.
2. Methods
The method section includes the description of the site (Section 2.1), 
the physics-based ATES model developed in MOOSE-GOLEM Frame-
work (Section 2.2), the key performance characteristics which lead 
to reduction of the model order to address model interference (Sec-
tion 2.3) and the model reduction (Section 2.4).
2.1. Study area
The ATES system considered in this study is analogous to the 
planned ATES in the southeast of Berlin district of Adlershof. This 
ATES utilizes fine-grained Jurassic sandstones to store and provide 
heat for the district heating network. The Hettang aquifer sediments 
are predominantly weakly consolidated, fine-grained sandstones with 
a high quartz content and varying organic fractions (coal flakes) [16]. 
The planned ATES will consist of two wells with filter zone penetrating 
the full aquifer thickness at the depth intervals 360 to 390 m (Fig.  1).
The ATES system in Berlin Adlershof is targeting an aquifer which 
has a thickness of 30 to 60 m and consists of transgression–regression 
cycles of clay, siltstones, and sandstones. The Hettang Jurassic aquifer 
is isolated from the above positioned artesian aquifer by the Rupelian 
clay layer with thickness variation from 40 to 120 m and the screened 
thickness at the Adlershof site is more than 100 m [42]. With the 
ambient temperature of 24 ◦C and high salinity, the targeted for HT-
ATES Hettang aquifer is well isolated from the artesian aquifer [43]. 
The Hettang aquifer is characterized by slow (less than 0.1 m/year) 
ambient groundwater velocity, which makes it plausible for geothermal 
storage utilization [44].
Preliminary site investigations, complemented by regional data, 
indicated that the permeability ranges from 1 ⋅ 10−13 to 1 ⋅ 10−12 m2, 
with porosity between 0.1 and 0.4 [16]. For modelling purposes, a 
permeability range of 1⋅10−14 to 5⋅10−12 m2 is considered to encompass 
most realistic porous aquifers suitable for ATES systems. To ensure a 
comprehensive approach, no empirical relationship between porosity 
and permeability was imposed, allowing these parameters to be treated 
independently. The initial assessment suggests that the Hettang aquifer 
at Adlershof is approximately 60 m thick, although it remains uncertain 
pending further drilling results. To account for lateral variations in 
aquifer thickness and associated uncertainties, a wide range of thick-
nesses from 10 to 100 m were considered in the study. The parameter 
ranges were extended to account for parametric uncertainty (Table  1).
The urban setting of the ATES site presents specific challenges. 
Due to the dense urbanization and limited access to the properties, 
the choice of well distance in Adlershof is limited. On the existing 
drilling site, the maximum distance possible in the reservoir depth is 
approximately 100 metres. Because of the complex ownership and leas-
ing conditions in the densely populated area, larger distances require 
additional approvals. Therefore, careful planning of the well placement 
is crucial to optimize the system’s efficiency while complying with regu-
latory requirements. From the technological perspective, the Adlershof 
site offers a range of possible technical solutions for the ATES system, 
as summarized in Table  1. The considered charging temperatures vary 
between 70 to 100 ◦C, and charging/extraction rates of 50 to 150 m3/h.
In such HT-ATES systems, optimizing the distance between wells 
is crucial for maximizing energy performance. Wells placed too close 
reduce pressure drop and improve hydraulic efficiency, but risk ther-
mal interference, which lowers energy recovery. Conversely, spacing 
wells too far apart minimizes thermal interference but increases flow 
resistance and drawdown, potentially violating hydraulic constraints. 
Thus, both minimum and maximum well distances must be considered 
to balance thermal and hydraulic performance.

To condition the model to the natural state, Dirichlet boundary con-
ditions were applied at the lateral and bottom boundaries to represent 
undisturbed geothermal conditions [45,46], while no-flow (Neumann) 
conditions are assumed at the top boundary to reflect low permeability 
of an aquitard. Internal boundary conditions for ATES are given by 
0.5 years injection and extraction cycles in warm and cold wells. The 
modelled system will focus on a basic ATES setup consisting of two 
wells penetrating the full aquifer thickness. The excessive hot water 
is injected into warm well to store the heat while at the same time, 
aquifer groundwater is extracted from the cold well. After half a year, 
the previously injected warm water is extracted from the warm well 
to provide heating, and the cooled (until aquifer temperature) water is 
injected into the cold well. Together, injection and extraction periods 
from a cycle which is repeated (for example, seasonally) during ATES 
functioning (Fig.  1).
The study focused on ATES where ambient groundwater flow is 
negligible. Lateral boundary conditions were based on global modelling 
results, considering both expected and observed data from nearby 
locations. No-flow boundary conditions were applied along the bottom 
and top horizontal boundaries to simulate impermeable rock layers. 
The aquifer was assumed to have homogeneous isotropic properties 
within the model domain.
The computational domain was discretized using a mesh of ver-
tically extruded triangular prisms, with horizontal spacing varying 
from 0.1 m around the wells to 50 m at the model’s boundary to 
ensure the high resolution around the well. This non-uniform grid 
was generated using the open-source software GMSH [47] (Fig.  2, 
left). Coupled flow and heat transport equations within porous media 
were solved using the finite element software MOOSE-GOLEM [48,
49]. The aquifer was simulated as a single material layer with ho-
mogeneous parameters (porosity, permeability, heat capacity). This 
simplification is commonly used to reduce model complexity and com-
putational load, especially at ATES planning stages when site-specific 
heterogeneity data is limited due to limited amount of deep boreholes 
reflecting on the spatial permeability–porosity distribution. Previous 
studies e.g., Frick et al. [46] show that homogeneous models effectively 
capture dominant transport behaviour. While small-scale features like 
layering or anisotropy are simplified, the approach offers a solid basis 
for system understanding and can be extended with spatial variability 
in future work. Density and viscosity were set temperature and pressure 
dependent updated according to IAPWS-97 [50]. For compliance, we 
neglected interactions with adjacent low hydraulic conductivity layers. 
Additionally, we did not consider storage periods where injection and 
extraction phases are separated by intervals of inactivity.
During the simulation, the hot water is injected at a constant 
flowrate into the aquifer while the ambient temperature water is pro-
duced from another well, and after 6 month the flow direction in 
the wells is reversed. The simulation included ten yearly cycles of 
continuous injection and extraction, each phase lasting six months. This 
10-year period was chosen based on convergence studies, which indi-
cate that system behaviour stabilizes over this time window [51]. The 
performed simulations were stabilizing within the 6 to 10 years period. 
We made use of an adaptive time stepping based on the computed 
Courant number for the system, with a default time step size of 1 day. 
Charging and extraction flowrates were kept constant throughout the 
simulation. Key model parameters, including porosity, permeability, 
charging temperatures, flowrates, aquifer thickness, and well spac-
ing are detailed further in Section 5. The model outputs included a 
fully 3D, spatio-temporally resolved field of temperature and pressure 
distributions (see Fig.  2, right).

3. Surrogate model setup and optimization
In Section 3.1, we present the workflow for ensemble generation 
using quasi-random sampling, with adjustments for key parameters. 
In Section 3.2, we detail the approach of training a Random Forest 
Classifier (RFC) and compute the probability of thermal interference, 
and outline the global sensitivity analysis technique. In Section 3.3, 
we describe the infill procedure and a confusion matrix as a quality 
assessment of the surrogate model.
3.1. Ensemble generation
The surrogate model has to cover all parametric space and reflect on 
the parameter connections of the physics-based model, which requires 
high prediction accuracy. We enable this by creating a relatively large 
ensemble of parameter combinations and sampling uniformly the para-
metric space. This is done by using a quasi-random Halton sequence 
with a uniform prior probability density function. Physical parameter 
values of the model range over different scales and have different units 
(Table  1).
The permeability and well distance values were log-transformed to 
smooth over the parameter space. In case of the well distance which 
varies from 50 to 400 m, we gain more samples from the small distance 
values, which tend to produce thermal interference. This way, the 
sampling resolution around small well distances was increased. Then, 
parameters were normalized in their ranges in order to homogenize 
each of them between 0 and 1. The model is constrained by the 
appearance of turbulent flow in the vicinity to the well. This was 
avoided by limiting the charging and extraction rates based on the 
Reynolds number.

In this study, we employed RFC to model a binary classification 
problem with six input parameters: permeability, porosity, aquifer 
thickness, charging temperature, flowrate, and distance between two 
wells. The algorithm [41] is an ensemble learning technique that 
constructs a multitude of decision trees during training and outputs 
the mode of the classes for classification tasks or the mean prediction 
for regression tasks. The RFC offers several advantages for our purpose 
in comparison to other ML methods. As such, RFC is faster to train 
than Gradient Boosting methods since it trains trees in parallel which 
speeds up the training, and has more intuitive hyperparameter tuning, 
yet allowing the sensitivity analysis [57,58]. The RFC handles larger 
datasets better than Support Vector Machines and does not necessarily 
require normalization, and finally, it is targeting to use categorical data 
which is the goal of the study [58–60]. This method is particularly 
effective in handling high-dimensional data and mitigates the risk of 
over-fitting.
The model input parameters were used as input features for the RFC 
with a binary output. We configured the RFC with 100 trees, where 
each tree was built using a subset of the data and features, selected 
through bootstrapping and random feature selection, respectively. The 
implementation of the Classifier was performed through the ‘‘Random-
ForestClassifier’’ function in the ‘‘sklearn’’ Python library [61].
To optimize model performance, the hyperparameters were tuned 
using Grid Search with cross validation [61]. Key parameters included 
the 100 of trees estimators, the maximum depth of each tree 10, and 
the minimum number of samples required to split an internal node was 
set to 2. For the tuning, we used the GridSearchCV function from the 
‘‘sklearn’’ package in Python [61], which allows for automated tuning 
of hyperparameters across specified parameter grids while also imple-
menting k-fold cross-validation to ensure robust model evaluation. We 
set the number of folds to 5, enabling a comprehensive assessment of 
model performance on different subsets of the training data.
Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) was used to determine the influ-
ence of input variables on the output of a model [62,63]. The Sobol 
sensitivity analysis was performed on the RFC using the SALib Python 
library [64]. First, Sobol samples were generated for the input variables 
using the Saltelli sampling method [65]. The model was then evaluated 
on these samples to obtain the output probabilities and compute the 
first-order (𝑆𝑖) and total-order (𝑆𝑇𝑖) Sobol indices. . In this study, the 
binary output of the RFC (0 or 1) is treated as a continuous probability 
output, to represent probability likelihood.

4.2. Surrogate model and sensitivity analysis
To validate the trained RFC, 20% of the models and their associated 
parameter combinations were used as a holdout dataset, which did not 
participate in the training process. This holdout set was exclusively 
used to evaluate the classifier’s performance.
The potential overfitting was excluded by k-fold cross-validation

mance and generalizability across the parameter space (Section 3.2). 
The validation results, illustrated in the form of a confusion matrix

This reflects a high accuracy of the selected approximation procedure

The Sobol sensitivity analysis [64] was performed on the RFC 
and technical and natural variables (Table  1). First, Sobol samples 
were generated for the input variables using the Saltelli sampling 
method [65]. The model was then evaluated on these samples to obtain 
the output probabilities and compute the first-order (𝑆𝑖) and total-order

distance as a variable. The results are depicted in Fig.  7.
Results of the full dataset (Fig.  7, top-left) confirm that the well 
distance has a first-order influence on thermal interference. The well 
distance has by far the highest sensitivity index of  0.9. The next 
influential parameters are geometry and hydraulic boundary condition 
of the aquifer, that is, thickness and charging flowrate.
To better resolve the effects of less dominant parameters, the same 
metrics computed excluding well distance from analysis, are depicted 
in Fig.  7, right panel. This procedure allows to avoid masking effects, 
as highly influential parameters can dominate the variance, making it 
difficult to detect the contributions of others [67]. First order sensitivity

When the well distance is fixed, thickness, and charging flowrate have 
the highest influence on the thermal interference. This makes sense

permeability, which share a similar result with 0.2.
The second-order sensitivity indices (Fig.  7, the bottom panels) also 
show the highest sensitivity for the well distance (bottom-left) along 
with the aquifer thickness. Besides the well distance, thickness together

recovery rates and reducing the overall costs associated with energy 
wastage and over-compensation through external energy sources.

5. Summary and discussion
This study presents a comprehensive approach to optimize ATES 
doublet systems, integrating a novel asymptotic approximation for HRF 
and SE with machine learning techniques, and presenting a robust 
methodology for predicting and mitigating thermal interference under 
varying geological and technical conditions. We introduced a novel 
asymptotic approximation for the time development of the HRF and 
SE in an ATES doublet system operating with constant six-month-long 
cycles. This approximation, validated across a broad range of input 
parameters, enables the reduction of a spatially resolved numerical 
model of ATES without sacrificing accuracy. Our detailed model anal-
ysis reveals that the time derivative of Stored Energy is a critical factor 
in determining optimal well spacing.
A key innovation of this work is the development of an RFC trained 
on an ensemble of spatially resolved numerical models. The trained 
classifier reflects on the parameter dependencies and allows stochastic 
prediction of the thermal interference and global sensitivity analy-
sis. The comparison with the conventional thermal radius approach 
(e.g. [9,27,68]) has demonstrated similarity with the RFC approach for 
a simple model (Section 4.3). While the typically applied thermal radius 
approach (Eq. (7)) is an effective and simple analytical estimate of the 
well distancing, it has several assumptions, such as simplified geology, 
constant boundary conditions, nonlinear effects, and long-term effects 
of ATES functioning. The physics-based model used to train RFC, on 
the contrary, is capable of capturing these effects and complex geology, 
which enables a precise estimate of reliable long-term ATES system 
performance. The outlined here approach provides a framework for 
the stochastic well distance evaluation while accounting for the model 
complexity while reducing computational cost by up to 10 times in 
comparison to Monte Carlo approaches. These results highlight the 
effectiveness of the proposed model in capturing the complex thermal 
interactions in ATES systems, suggesting that in urbanized areas it 
may be profitable to implement detailed simulations in order to decide 
about optimal well distance. The model considered in this study serves 
as a demonstration of the applicability of this approach for more 
complex geological or technical conditions, providing a tool for the 
uncertainty-acknowledged planning of ATES.
The modelling framework was applied to the planned ATES in Berlin 
Adlershof, Germany. The result of probabilistic computations for an 
ATES doublet shows that the probability of the thermal interference 
is 1 for small well distances and is constantly decreasing to 0 for 
the distance between the wells more than 130 m. The Productivity 
Index consideration, which takes into account the hydraulic response 
of the aquifer, suggests a maximum well distance of 160 m. Considered 
together, hydraulic and thermal characteristics significantly narrow 
down the possible range of well spacings which has to be considered 
in planning ATES in urban areas. Based on such estimates, the optimal 
well spacing at the Adlershof site lies between 130 m and 160 m.
While the proposed model offers improvements in fast evaluation 
of the optimal well placement for ATES under parametric uncertainty, 
several limitations must be acknowledged to contextualize the results 
and inform future research.
The model assumes homogeneous aquifer properties such as per-
meability and porosity, which may not be representative of the highly 
heterogeneous geological environments where ATES systems are im-
plemented [12]. Although the model accounts for a broad range of 
parameter values, real-world aquifers may exhibit parameter variability 
beyond the considered ranges. This can lead to discrepancies between 
model predictions and actual system performance, especially in aquifers 
with strong stratification or fractures. Future studies should incorporate 
more advanced geological characterization, including field data on 
heterogeneity and anisotropy, to improve model accuracy.
The model neglected the influence of ambient groundwater flow, 
which may be non-negligible for shallow aquifers [15]. In addition, the 
model does not account for long-term conduction through the aquitard. 
By focusing primarily on advection and dispersion within the aquifer, 
the model may underestimate the total thermal losses, especially over 
extended storage periods. Including these conductive effects in future 
iterations of the model would provide a more comprehensive under-
standing of the long-term energy recovery efficiency. Even considering 
very slow ambient groundwater flow in the Adlershof [44,46], the next 
steps in site characterization therefore include groundwater isotope 
sampling and corresponding dating, geophysics, and tracer tests to 
quantify the seepage velocity.
The model operates on the assumption of consistent operational 
cycles, with fixed injection and extraction periods of equal duration (six 
months). In reality, seasonal variations in energy demand, groundwater 
flow, and ambient temperatures can significantly impact the perfor-
mance of ATES systems [26]. These factors may lead to suboptimal 
system operation if they are not considered during the design phase. A 
future extension of the model should explore how seasonal and climate-
related variability affects ATES efficiency, enabling more adaptive and 
resilient system designs.
While the model successfully optimizes technical parameters, it does 
not account for economic constraints or regulatory requirements that 
often influence the feasibility of ATES projects [21]. Factors such as 
drilling costs, land ownership disputes, and regulatory compliance for 
well placement in urban areas can significantly alter the viability of a 
given design. Integrating economic models and policy frameworks into 
the simulation  would allow for more realistic feasibility assessments.
Broader validation against a range of real-world ATES systems is 
necessary to generalize the findings. Since the geological and technical 
settings can vary widely between sites, further field validation in di-
verse geological contexts is essential to confirm the model’s robustness 
and adaptability.
While the current model provides a robust framework for optimizing 
ATES system design, particularly in urban settings, future work must 
address these limitations to improve its real-world applicability. Incor-
porating more detailed geological data, accounting for long-term vari-
ability of the charging temperature and charging/extraction flowrates,

6. Conclusions
The key findings and novelty of this study can be described as 
follows:
- The developed analytical asymptotic approximations are capable 
to precisely mimic Heat Recovery Factor and Stored Energy decade-
scale evolution for a 6-month injection/withdrawal cycles of ATES over 
a broad parameter range.
- The developed Random Forest Classifier reflects on the parameter 
dependencies and allows stochastic prediction of the thermal interfer-
ence and global sensitivity analysis under possible natural or technical 
uncertainties. In comparison to conventionally used thermal radius ap-
proach, Random Forest Classifier methodology is based on ensemble of 
physics-based models which can capture complex geology and dynamic 
conditions, providing a robust framework for reliable well distance 
planning in urbanized areas under parametric uncertainty.
- Until now, only the thermal consideration has been considered 
to identify the minimum distance. We have shown that the hydraulic 
consideration also helps to identify  the maximum distance between 
the wells leading to the optimal well placement. Based on the thermal 
and hydraulic considerations for Berlin Adlershof, the optimal distance 
between the wells should be between 130 and 160 m. For optimal well 
design, both constraints have to be considered.
- The well spacing recommendation derived from ensemble simula-
tions is probabilistically bounded and reflects a risk-informed decision 
framework based on RFC-derived probabilities.
- The global sensitivity analysis reveals that influential parame-
ters for thermal interference are (descending order): well placement 
(by far), aquifer thickness, charging flowrate, charging temperature, 
permeability, and porosity. The model’s limitations stem from the 
assumptions made for the spatially resolved model, the considered pa-
rameters, and their ranges. However, these constraints do not diminish 
the model’s value in advancing ATES design.
The study developed a generic methodology for urban planners 
and engineers for rapid and accurate feasibility assessments of ATES 
systems under various geological and technical conditions. The Ran-
dom Forest Classifier can be integrated into spatial planning tools to 
rapidly evaluate geothermal well-spacing scenarios under technical and 
natural uncertainties. The Random Forest Classifier allows for real-time 
screening of design alternatives, supporting zoning decisions, energy 
district planning, and changing strategies in urban environments.  The 
approach enhances the efficiency and reliability of ATES systems, par-
ticularly in densely urbanized areas where optimal well placement is 
crucial for minimizing energy loss and maximizing recovery efficiency.
